title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Seattle, WA: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Seattle welders and QC staff: WABO special inspection route, D1.1 and D1.8, Part B planning. Online or at your facility.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Preparation in Seattle: a Six-Day Course for Puget Sound Welders and Inspectors
html:
Seattle builds and repairs ships, supplies parts to aircraft assembly lines, floats a highway across Lake Washington and puts up steel-framed towers in an earthquake zone. Each of those jobs needs people who can read a weld, a shop drawing and a code book with the same confidence. Atlantis NDT offers a six-day course that gets Puget Sound welders, fitters, quality control staff, NDT technicians and engineers ready to sit the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) examination. A candidate on their own studies online, following a written study plan with course materials and practice questions, and sends questions to an instructor when they get stuck. A Seattle employer with several people to prepare can instead have the six days run inside its own shop, yard or plant.

The American Welding Society (AWS) runs the CWI examination, scores it and issues the certificate. Atlantis prepares candidates and stops there: it certifies nobody, never sees the exam, and is not approved or endorsed by AWS. You meet the AWS education and experience requirements and pass the AWS vision test on your own. The day-by-day outline lives on the AWS CWI exam prep course page. This page is about how the course fits Seattle, King County and the wider Sound.

The WABO route: why a CWI counts on Washington building sites

In most states, the link between CWI certification and building construction runs through the special inspection chapter of the International Building Code. Washington adds a layer of its own. The Washington Association of Building Officials (WABO) registers special inspection agencies and the inspectors who work for them, and its Standard 1701 (21st edition, effective July 2024) sets out who qualifies. "Structural Welding" is one of the inspector categories in that standard.

For structural welding, Standard 1701 recognises two certificate routes. The first is an ICC structural welding certificate, which a candidate can earn through the ICC S2 written exam or by holding an AWS D1.1 CWI. The second is an AWS D1.1 CWI combined with plan-reading experience. In both routes the CWI is a direct way into structural welding special inspection in Washington.

It is not the whole requirement, and nobody should sell it as one. WABO also asks for employment with a WABO-registered agency, a recommendation letter from an official of that agency, a list of projects you have worked on, a points total built from education and recent special inspection experience, and an oral interview on field experience, codes and testing procedures. A candidate who passes the CWI exam still has that registration process ahead of them.

The practical consequence for exam planning is simple. A Seattle candidate aiming at special inspection should take Part C on AWS D1.1, because the WABO wording ties the CWI route to that code. A candidate headed for pipeline or pressure-equipment work may choose a different book, which the code-book section below covers.

Where Puget Sound welds get inspected

The welding work around Seattle is more varied than in most metros of its size, and that variety decides which parts of the CWI body of knowledge matter most to a local candidate.

  • Shipbuilding and ship repair. Vigor runs a shipyard on Harbor Island in Elliott Bay, the former Todd Pacific yard, where Washington State Ferries vessels have been built and maintained. Across the Sound, Puget Sound Naval Shipyard in Bremerton maintains Navy ships and submarines. Navy work follows NAVSEA technical publications, under which the yard qualifies its own inspectors, so a CWI is useful background in Bremerton but does not replace the Navy qualification.
  • Aerospace supply chain. Boeing assembles airplanes in Renton and Everett, and hundreds of suppliers around them machine, form and weld components. Airframe structure is mostly fastened rather than welded, but ducting, brackets, ground support equipment, tooling and engine-related hardware are welded to AWS D17.1 or to a customer specification. AWS offers a D17.1 endorsement for CWIs who want to show competence in that code.
  • Bridges and transit. WSDOT's SR 520 floating bridge, Sound Transit's light rail extensions and the region's steel overpasses all involve structural or bridge welding. Bridge fabrication follows AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, and a D1.5 endorsement exists for inspectors who work on it.
  • Towers in a seismic zone. Steel moment frames and braced frames in Seattle buildings are designed for earthquakes. That brings in AWS D1.8, the seismic supplement to D1.1, with its demand-critical welds, notch-tough filler metals and tighter rules on certain joints. A D1.1 CWI who has also read D1.8 is more useful on a downtown high-rise than one who has not.
  • Port, refinery and industrial work. Container terminals and their cranes, cold-storage plants and the industrial strip along the Duwamish Waterway create steady repair welding. North of the city, the refineries in Skagit and Whatcom counties run maintenance and turnaround programs that pull welders and inspectors up the I-5 corridor.

Put together, a Seattle CWI candidate needs a broader base than a candidate in a single-industry town. The common thread is D1.1 structural steel, with the other codes layered on top depending on where you work.

Who hires CWIs around Seattle, and what each employer checks

Seattle-area CWI job postings come from a handful of employer types. Knowing which one you want to work for changes how you prepare.

  • Special inspection and testing agencies registered with WABO send inspectors to building and transit projects for the owner. They want a D1.1 CWI who can also clear the WABO registration steps and write a clean daily inspection report.
  • Structural steel fabricators and erectors, many of them AISC-certified, employ in-house quality control inspectors who check fit-up, preheat, weld size, profile and finished dimensions before the owner's inspector ever sees the piece. These employers value speed with a fillet gauge and fluency with welding symbols.
  • Shipyards and marine contractors doing commercial hull, deck and outfitting work need inspectors who can move between AWS codes, class society rules and owner specifications. Atlantis can support marine programs through maritime NDT consulting for Seattle as well.
  • Aerospace and precision manufacturers welding to D17.1 want inspectors who are comfortable with small parts, tight tolerances and visual acceptance under magnification.
  • Utility and energy contractors doing gas distribution and transmission work inspect to API 1104 and want candidates who chose that book or plan to add the pipeline endorsement.
  • Inspection and NDT companies pair CWI visual inspection with ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant testing. Atlantis sends technicians to customer sites for weld inspection in Seattle, and the same combination of visual and NDT skills is what these firms look for when they hire.

One distinction trips up new inspectors. A fabricator's QC inspector works for the fabricator and checks its own product. A special inspector works for the owner or the building official and verifies that the work meets the approved documents. Both may hold a CWI, but they answer to different people and sign different records. The course discusses that difference on Day 2, where inspector duties and ethics are covered.

The Puget Sound Olympic Section of AWS

AWS organizes its members into districts and local sections. Seattle-area members belong to the Puget Sound Olympic Section in AWS District 19; the same district has a Spokane section on the east side of the state. Local sections hold technical meetings, plant tours, student events and scholarship programs. For a CWI candidate, a section meeting is the quickest way to meet working inspectors who can tell you which code book local employers prefer, how they documented their own experience, and what the practical part of the exam felt like on the day.

Section officers and meeting places change from year to year, so look up the District 19 page on aws.org for current contacts rather than relying on an old flyer.

Learning to weld in Seattle: South Seattle College and WABO welder tests

Many Seattle CWI candidates started as welders, and a good number came through the Welding Fabrication Technology program at South Seattle College. The college also runs WABO welder certification tests, which matter locally because WABO certifies structural welders as well as registering special inspectors. Its test menu covers GMAW and gas-shielded FCAW on vertical and overhead plate, SMAW and GTAW on plate and on 6G pipe, and a D1.8 seismic certification. The college itself warns candidates that the test is very difficult unless they regularly run multi-pass groove welds in heavy plate.

That background helps on the CWI exam in two ways. A welder who has taken a WABO bend test already understands why root opening, bevel angle and backing matter, which makes the joint-design and discontinuity questions in Part A feel familiar. A welder who has watched coupons crack on the bend jig knows what lack of fusion looks like, which is a large part of the practical. The usual gap is the paperwork side: welding symbols to AWS A2.4, terminology to AWS A3.0, WPS and PQR documents, and quick navigation through a code book. That is where the six days put most of their weight.

If you want a refresher on how procedure and welder qualification documents relate to each other before you start, read the WPS, PQR and WPQ guide. Atlantis does not write or qualify welding procedures, but candidates must be able to read them.

Sitting the CWI exam from Seattle

The CWI exam has three parts, and they are not all taken in the same place.

  • Part A, Fundamentals: 150 questions, computer-based, taken at a Prometric test center.
  • Part B, Practical: hands-on tasks with AWS-provided equipment plus 46 related questions, held at AWS seminar locations on dates linked to the seminar calendar.
  • Part C, Code Application: an open-book computer test of 50 to 65 questions on one approved code book, also at Prometric.

Prometric has over 100 US centers according to AWS, so a Seattle candidate can normally book Parts A and C locally after AWS mails the confirmation letter carrying the eligibility code Prometric wants. Part B is the part to plan around. Check aws.org for the nearest seminar location and its dates before you fix a study timeline, because a Puget Sound candidate may need to travel for it. AWS requires at least 72% on each part, and the parts are scored separately.

The article on CWI results by part shows where candidates tend to drop marks. Exam and seminar fees are set by AWS and listed on aws.org; to total up a Part B trip, code book purchases and unpaid days, work through the CWI exam spending planner.

Choosing your Part C code book for Washington work

AWS lets you bring one approved code book into Part C. Its current list includes AWS D1.1 (2020 edition), API 1104 (22nd edition) and ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section IX (2023 edition). Confirm the edition list on aws.org before you buy, because AWS updates it.

Code bookWhere it fits around Puget SoundNotes for local candidates
AWS D1.1WABO special inspection, steel fabrication shops, transit stations, port structures, towersThe default choice for most Seattle candidates and the one the WABO route names. Read the D1.8 seismic supplement alongside it.
API 1104Gas distribution and transmission construction, terminal pipingUseful if you already work for a utility contractor; the pipeline endorsement can be added later if you start on D1.1.
ASME Section IXPressure vessel shops, boiler work, refinery maintenance in Skagit and Whatcom countiesSection IX covers qualification, not acceptance criteria for production welds, so expect qualification-heavy questions.

Before Day 4, skim the site's summary of the structural steel code and its walk-through of how D1.1 accepts or rejects a weld. Pipeline candidates should start with the API 1104 overview.

How the six days work for a Seattle candidate

The course covers the AWS body of knowledge in six blocks. Here is how each block tends to land for someone working in this region.

  1. Fundamentals I. Welding processes, joint design, AWS A3.0 terms and AWS A2.4 symbols. Seattle candidates often bring shop drawings for moment-frame connections, which make the symbol drills concrete.
  2. Fundamentals II. Metallurgy, mechanical testing, discontinuities and their causes, destructive and nondestructive testing, safety, and inspector duties and ethics. Notch toughness gets extra time because of seismic work.
  3. Practical. Measuring and gauging, weld size and profile, and visual acceptance against a book of specifications. Groups trained at the employer's site can use their own gauges and weld samples; Atlantis does not ship replica kits.
  4. Code application. Finding your way through the code book you chose: clause structure, tables, acceptance criteria and qualification requirements.
  5. Timed practice. Practice exams for Parts A, B and C under time pressure, followed by review of every missed question.
  6. Weak-area review and exam-day planning. Targeted revision, how to pace each part, and a checklist for the AWS application and supporting documents.

Practice questions are original and written to the published body of knowledge; they are never real AWS exam questions. Solo candidates fit the material around shifts and message the instructor with questions as they go. A fabricator in Kent or a marine contractor on the Duwamish with a handful of people preparing together can keep them on site and have the six days taught there instead of sending staff away. The course outlines what will be taught; it does not promise a result on the exam.

Eligibility notes for Puget Sound welders and inspectors

AWS trades education against welding-related work experience on a sliding scale, and the full table is on the national course page. For most Seattle candidates, three rows matter. A welder who finished high school or holds an equivalent needs five years of welding-related work. Someone who completed trade or vocational welding courses, such as a college welding certificate, needs four. A graduate of a two-year engineering technology, engineering or physical science program needs two. Degree holders in welding engineering or welding technology need one, and candidates with less schooling need nine or twelve years.

Two local situations come up again and again. Naval and commercial shipyard welders often have long careers but little paperwork outside the yard's own records, so start gathering employer letters and supervisor contacts months before you apply. Aerospace technicians may have spent years inspecting rather than welding; AWS alone decides whether that counts as welding-related, so read its definition before you count on it. Every candidate must also pass the AWS vision test on the current AWS form. The article on CWI requirements and career impact goes deeper into documentation.

After the exam: endorsements and next steps in the region

Once issued, a CWI runs on a nine-year clock according to AWS, punctuated by renewal paperwork in the third and sixth years. At year nine the options AWS lists include retaking Part B, documenting 80 professional development hours, or holding Certified Radiographic Interpreter status. Endorsements that suit Seattle work include D1.5 bridge welding, D17.1 aerospace, API 1104 pipeline, and the magnetic particle and penetrant testing endorsements. Some inspectors later work toward Senior CWI; the Senior CWI pathway article explains that step.

Many CWIs also add NDT methods. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies NDT personnel, and Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A-based training for that purpose: see VT Level II training and the wider NDT training options for Seattle. The comparison of CWI, API 577 and ASNT Level II sets out how the credentials differ. Simulated weld practice is available through Practical NDT's welding workshop.

Candidates in neighboring markets can compare notes on the Portland CWI prep page, the Salt Lake City page and the Denver page.

Ask for a quote for Seattle candidates or crews

Send a short note with the number of people preparing, the code book each intends to use, whether you want individual online access or the six days at your facility, and the city where that facility is. A rough idea of each person's experience helps too. Use the AWS CWI exam prep quote form for Seattle, and Atlantis will reply within one business day.

faq.q: Does a CWI let me work as a structural welding special inspector in Washington?
faq.a: It is one of the accepted routes. WABO Standard 1701 recognises an AWS D1.1 CWI (on its own as a route to the ICC certificate, or combined with plan-reading experience) for the Structural Welding category. WABO also requires employment with a registered agency, a recommendation letter, a points total from education and experience, and an oral interview.

faq.q: Which code book should a Seattle candidate choose for Part C?
faq.a: Most choose AWS D1.1, because building, transit and port work runs on it and the WABO route names it. Utility and pipeline workers may prefer API 1104, and pressure vessel or refinery maintenance staff sometimes choose ASME Section IX. Check the current edition list on aws.org.

faq.q: Where do Seattle candidates take the CWI exam?
faq.a: You book Fundamentals and Code Application at a Prometric center once AWS issues your eligibility code; both are taken on a computer. Part B is held at AWS seminar locations on set dates, so check aws.org for the nearest site; you may need to travel for it.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Seattle?
faq.a: No. A candidate studying alone works online and sends questions to an instructor, while a Seattle-area employer can host the six days at its plant or yard for its own people. Atlantis keeps offices in Houston and Hyderabad and nowhere else.

faq.q: Does Atlantis certify me as a CWI?
faq.a: No. AWS administers the examination and issues the CWI certification. Atlantis prepares you for it and is not approved or endorsed by AWS. You must meet the AWS eligibility rules and pass the vision test yourself.

faq.q: I weld at a naval shipyard. Does my CWI replace the Navy inspector qualification?
faq.a: No. Navy work follows NAVSEA technical publications, and the yard qualifies its own inspectors under them. A CWI is useful background and is widely recognised in commercial work, but it does not substitute for the yard qualification.

faq.q: Is AWS D1.8 covered in the course?
faq.a: The course is built on the CWI body of knowledge and your chosen code book. Seattle groups working on seismic steel can ask for D1.8 examples to be used in the symbol, metallurgy and visual acceptance exercises, since D1.8 supplements D1.1.

faq.q: Are the practice questions taken from the real exam?
faq.a: No. They are original questions written to the published AWS body of knowledge. They are never copies of AWS exam questions.

faq.q: How long is the CWI certificate valid?
faq.a: AWS gives the certificate a nine-year life. Paperwork renewals fall in years three and six, and at year nine you recertify through Part B, professional development hours or CRI status. See the national CWI prep page for more.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for a group in Seattle?
faq.a: Use the Seattle CWI quote form with the number of candidates, their code books and your facility location. Atlantis replies within one business day.
